MINUTES OF A REGULAR MEETING OF THE LOMITA CITY COUNCIL
October 7, 2013

1.  OPENING CEREMONIES

a.  Call Meeting to Order

A regular meeting of the Lomita City Council was called to order at 7:00 p.m., on
Monday, October 7, 2013, in the Council Chambers, at Lomita City Hall, 24300
Narbonne Avenue.

b.  Flag Salute

Councilmember Traina led the salute to the flag.

c.  Invocation

Councilmember Sanchez gave the invocation.

d.  Roll Call

Those responding to roll call by Assistant City Clerk Shumway were
COUNCILMEMBERS: Gazeley, Traina, Savidan, Sanchez, and Mayor Estrada. Also
present were City Manager Rock, Assistant City Manager Sugano, City Attorney Hogin,
Public Works Director Damasse, Community Services Director McPherron, Parks and
Recreation Director Harding, Administrative Services Director Chavez, and Assistant
City Clerk Shumway.

2.  APPROVAL OF AGENDA

Councilmember Savidan moved to approve the agenda.  Councilmember Sanchez
seconded the motion, which carried unanimously.

5. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS

None.

6. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS AND MEETING ATTENDANCE REPORTS FROM THE
  CITY COUNCIL

In response to Councilmember Traina’s questions whether there is a City ordinance that
regulates parking in driveways, specifically pertaining to cars that block sidewalks, and

  Page 1
 what options are available to residents in order to deal with such issues, Assistant City
Manager Sugano responded that such violations fall under code enforcement, but in
order for such violations to be remedied, residents need to contact the City and file a
complaint, as those types of code violations are not part of the proactive code
enforcement.

Councilmember Traina stated that crews were working at night on Eshelman Avenue
flushing fire hydrants, and he asked whether it was routine maintenance, to which City
Manager Rock responded that flushing fire hydrants was routine water system
maintenance.

Councilmember Savidan reported that he attended the Lomita Sheriff’s Station Open
House, which was well attended.

Councilmember Gazeley requested a motion for a future agenda item to place a
moratorium on any future massage parlors, and recommended that staff start enforcing
the massage facilities ordinance with the ultimate goal of limiting the number of
massage businesses in the City of Lomita. Councilmember Traina, Sanchez, and
Savidan agreed to place this discussion item on a future Council agenda.

7. CITY MANAGER’S REPORT

City Manager Rock provided an update on the Cypress Water Production Facility
(CWPF), and stated that the CWPF continues to operate well with a 60/40
Metropolitan/Well water blend, and that the City’s water currently meets all primary
drinking standards, while many other cities have both harder water and higher TDS
levels than Lomita. Furthermore, City Manager Rock emphasized that the City cannot
rely solely on imported water, and that it is essential for the City to have its own reliable
water source for residents and business.

City Manager Rock clarified that the only salaries paid out of the Gas Tax Fund are
those for staff and crew members that actually allocate their time working on gas tax
eligible projects and associated activities.

In an update on scavenging related to recyclables, City Manager Rock stated that staff
and the LA County Sheriff’s Department are doing more enforcement and patrolling,
which in turn has resulted in the arrest of one repeat offender in the City.

City Manager Rock stated that the City will see the effects of the federal shutdown, as
the Housing and Urban Development (HUD) subsidy currently received by the City
would have to be covered through the use of City funds, with the hope that the City will
be reimbursed at a later time.

  Page 2
 8. CONSENT AGENDA

Councilmember Gazeley moved to approve the Consent Agenda.  Councilmember
Sanchez seconded the motion, which carried unanimously.

  a. Motion to Waive Further Reading.

  b. Recommendation to approve the minutes for the Regular City Council meeting
  held on September 16, 2013. RECOMMEND APPROVAL.

  c. Approval of Demands. RECOMMEND APPROVAL.

  d. Monthly Report for the Administrative Services Department. RECEIVE AND FILE.

  e. Monthly Report for the Community Development Department.  RECEIVE AND
  FILE.

  f. Monthly Report for the Parks and Recreation Department. RECEIVE AND FILE.

  g. Monthly Report for the Public Works Department. RECEIVE AND FILE.

  h. Monthly Report regarding Economic Development Activities. RECEIVE AND FILE.

  i. August 2013 Treasurer’s Report. RECEIVE AND FILE.

  j. Approval of an Ordinance repealing and replacing Chapter 8 (Massage) of Title VI
  of the Lomita Municipal Code in order to ensure consistency with State Law and
  enhance the City’s ability to regulate massage facilities and technicians operating
  within the City of Lomita. RECOMMEND APPROVAL.

  k. Approval of an Agreement between the City of Lomita and the City of Torrance for
  Torrance’s cost reimbursement of the design, construction, construction
  management, and construction inspection services in the amount of $218,549.10,
  for the Crenshaw/Lomita Boulevard Intersection Improvement Project.
  RECOMMEND APPROVAL.

  l. Authorize submittal of a letter to METRO regarding the monthly maintenance fee
  for transponder use on the Express Lanes. RECOMMEND APPROVAL.

  PUBLIC HEARING:
3.  HOUSING ELEMENT UPDATE

Veronica Tam provided a PowerPoint presentation (Attachment 1), and stated that the
Housing Element is one of seven mandated elements of the General Plan. According to
Ms. Tam, the primary purpose of the Housing Element is to identify current and future
housing needs, and the measures necessary to mitigate and alleviate those needs. Ms.

  Page 3
 Tam continued by stating that the Housing Element must be reviewed by the California
State Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for compliance with
state laws, and that the submission deadline for the 2013-2021 Housing Element is
October 15, 2013. Ms. Tam went on to further state that the goal of submitting the
Housing Element on time is so that the City can be found in substantial compliance in
order for the City to be eligible for State housing funds, as well as protection during
potential litigation. Finally, Ms. Tam stated that the revised Housing Element updates all
the information contained in the prior Housing Element, and also incorporates the
amendment to the Municipal Code regarding the requirements for emergency shelters
and other forms of supportive housing.

Mayor Estrada opened the Public Hearing.

George Kivett, Lomita resident, recommended that the City consider keeping low
density in residential zones, while higher density developments should only be
approved on Narbonne Avenue or Lomita Boulevard.  Furthermore, Mr. Kivett
recommended that City Council consider directing staff to review the entire General
Plan, as the last review was only done for mixed use, thrift stores, and the business
corridor.

Mayor Estrada closed the Public Hearing.

Councilmember Savidan moved that City Council authorize staff to submit the Draft
2013-2021 Housing Element to the California State Housing and Community
Development Department for review. Councilmember Gazeley seconded the motion,
which carried unanimously.

4.  ISLAMIC  CENTER  OF  THE  SOUTH  BAY  MOSQUE FACILITY
  REDEVELOPMENT APPLICATION (GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT NO. 2013-
  01, ZONE CHANGE NO. 2013-01, ZONE TEXT AMENDMENT NO. 2013-04,
  CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 282, ZONE VARIANCE NO. 233 AND
  MITIGATED NEGATIVE DECLARATION NO. 2013-03).

Councilmember Sanchez recused himself from discussion on this item as he lives within
500 feet from the subject property; Councilmember Sanchez left the Council Chambers.

Principal Planner Velasco provided a PowerPoint presentation (Attachment 2), and
stated that this is the second application that has been submitted proposing the
redevelopment of the site. According to Ms. Velasco, the first application was submitted
in 2009, and was denied by the City Council in March 2010, due to traffic and parking
concerns, the loss of commercial land, and the irregular shape of the parcel. Ms.
Velasco went on to state that the current project has been significantly changed from

  Page 4
 the 2009 project, when the Islamic Center of the South Bay acquired additional property
on Appian Way, which in turn added 20 more parking spaces, and the newly submitted
project is being proposed on a more standard, rectangular shaped lot. Ms. Velasco
continued by stating that the Planning Commission recommended approval of the
proposed project with additional conditions, and provided an overview of the proposed
project, including added conditions. According to Ms. Velasco, religious facilities are not
permitted in the C-R Zone, although the current use of the property is a legally non-
conforming religious facility, and the applicant (the Islamic Center of the South Bay) is
proposing a General Plan Amendment/Zone Change for the site to a Low Density
Residential/R-1 designation, where religious facilities are conditionally permitted, and as
a result of such changes in the General Plan and zoning, the existing non-conformity
would be eliminated. Furthermore, according to Ms. Velasco, staff added another
condition that the applicant prepare and submit for approval a parking management
program in order to mitigate findings regarding on-site and off-site parking, and the
accommodation of visitors without using neighborhood parking spaces.

City Attorney Hogin provided an overview and explanation of the City Council’s powers
and limitations regarding land use, as well as a brief description of Religious Land Use
and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA). According to City Attorney Hogin, the City
Council can create the laws that are in favor of the public welfare, but such laws cannot
be in conflict with State law. Furthermore, City Attorney Hogin stated that according to
RLUIPA, local governments cannot impose land regulations that can impose a
substantial burden on a religious institution to exercise their religious freedom.

Also, City Attorney Hogin provided an overview of the previous project denial and
lawsuit filed against the City by the applicant and the Department of Justice, as well as
the changes made to the project for tonight’s’ discussion.

Councilmember Traina stated that he reviewed the staff report, including the letters in
support and in opposition of the project, and asked whether the recommendations to
minimize the effects of the project to residential areas were taken into consideration and
discussed with the applicant, to which Assistant City Manager Sugano responded that
some of the recommendations were discussed with the applicant’s architect and it was
agreed that the number of doors on the east side would be reduced to two doors and
that the domes could consist of tinted glass.

In response to Councilmember Traina’s question on whether the parking management
program was approved in order to accommodate the 39 additional parking spaces,
Assistant City Manager Sugano responded that the applicant has agreed to the
recommendations in order to accommodate those items.

Anne Richardson, Attorney for the Islamic Center of the South Bay, stated that since

  Page 5
 2009, and throughout the length of the project, the Islamic Center of the South Bay has
talked to residents and members of the community, and has made the necessary
revisions to the project. Furthermore, Ms. Richardson added that the Department of
Justice and the Islamic Center of the South Bay agreed to the settlement pending the
resolution of the revised project coming in front of the City Council. Ms. Richardson
concluded by showing pictures of the current conditions at the Islamic Center of the
South Bay, which in turn are burdening this institution’s right to exercise their religion,
and added that the applicant has made numerous changes in response to resident
requests.

Shakil Patel, Architect for the Islamic Center of the South Bay, provided an overview of
the floor plan, and the changes made since the last application. According to Mr. Patel,
the proposed changes/additions to the facility are very neighbor-friendly, with no
geological issues, adds a visual screen between the Islamic Center and the residential
area by increasing the wall from 3 to 6 feet, new trees along the wall, reducing the
number of doors, and that all glass be tinted and shaded as part of the domes.
Furthermore, Mr. Patel stated that core samples were taken and the results were
satisfactory.

Discussion followed regarding the height and glass material of the domes, as well as
the number of doors and their proposed height. Councilmember Traina suggested that
doors not be higher than six feet.

In response to Councilmember Traina’s question as to whether core samples were
taken, Mr. Patel responded that core samples were taken at each phase of the study by
professional geologists and that nothing was encountered.

Councilmember Traina suggested that the wall be built prior to construction in order to
buffer the residents from any effects, such as dust and noise.

Mayor Estrada opened the Public Hearing.

Donna Palm, Lomita resident, recommended that the proposed domes be designed in a
flat manner in order to reduce glare, and that the domes be the same height, 27 feet, as
the rest of the building, which is in accordance with the Lomita Municipal Code.
Furthermore, Ms. Palm stated that the wall should be between eight and nine feet tall.

Reem Salahi, member of the public, stated that the Islamic Center could be 35 feet in
height without any variance according to the Lomita Municipal Code and in accordance
with the commercial/retail zoning of the property. Ms. Salahi went on to state that the
City has approved multiple variances in the past, and asked City Council to approve the

  Page 6
 project, which in turn would eliminate the hardship on the mosque so that their religion
can be exercised in adequate facilities.

Steve Gilliland, Bishop at the Church of Jesus Crist of Latter Day Saints, spoke as a
private citizen in support of the proposed property renovation, and emphasized that the
Islamic Center needs an adequate setting and facility to continue teaching their future
generations.

Judy Gilliand, member of the public, asked that Council approve the proposed
renovations to the Islamic Center of the South Bay.

Roni Love, congregate of the Temple of Israel in Long Beach, stated that she supports
the renovation of the Islamic Center of the South Bay, as they currently have an
inadequate facility.

Faiz Ali, Lomita resident, asked Council to approve the project, stated that the current
lack of space limits both her responsibilities and opportunities to participate and
organize associated events.

AK Mahida, member of the public, asked Council to approve the proposed project, and
stated that the community of Muslims is very respectful and neighborly, and that the
Islamic Center of the South Bay has never had any complaints from other members of
the community.

Jim Palm, Lomita resident, stated that the comments made by the attorney for the
Islamic Center of the South Bay are not true, as the Center has never worked with or
discussed issues with residents, except for one time. Mr. Palm expressed his concern
that his property value would decrease if the project is approved. Furthermore, Mr.
Palm asked that an eight to nine foot wall be built, and that the proposed height of the
doors be lowered to seven feet. Lastly, Mr. Palm asked that a traffic study be
conducted on Fridays during service at the Islamic Center, and that a noise study be
performed during Ramadan events.

Annes Rhoman, Lomita resident, stated that he was an established individual working
for Deloitte & Touche, and thanked the Islamic Center of the South Bay for helping him
to develop both professionally and spiritually. Mr. Rhoman also asked that Council
allow for the practice of their religion in an adequate facility.

Khlid Majidi, member of the public, asked Council to approve the project, as the current
condition of the facility is not to standard.

Ehtesham Mirza, member of the public, asked Council to approve the renovations for

  Page 7
 the Islamic Center of the South Bay, and further stated that the newly proposed project
meets City requirements, and that the proposed renovation would be a substantial
improvement.

Marc Everlove, member of the public, stated that the attorney fees associated with the
proposed project are high, and that that money could have been used for other things in
Lomita, which would have benefited the City.

David Popelka, Lomita Planning Commissioner, but speaking as a private citizen of
Lomita, stated that Council’s decision was already predetermined, as the lawsuit would
surface again without approval of the project. Mr. Popelka stated that when this matter
came in front of the Planning Commission he voted to oppose this project strictly based
on a land use basis. Mr. Popelka went on to state that the project is inconsistent with
zoning regulations, and that the applicant is asking for more variances than any other
project in the City. Mr. Popelka added that even when the Planning Commission
approved the project, someone from the public yelled obscenities, and he later received
phone calls threatening his family and was called a racist. According to Mr. Popelka,
this issue became a religious issue and Muslim groups state that they are being
discriminated against. In their own countries, no other religions are allowed to practice,
and other minority groups are oppressed. Mr. Popelka stated his opposition to the
approval of the project.

Nancy Sanchez, Lomita resident, stated that the reason her family moved to Lomita 38
years ago was that they liked the feeling of the small community. Ms. Sanchez stated
that her main concern was the size of the proposed building, and she suggested that
the building be built on a smaller scale, which would in turn fit the current zoning of the
area. Furthermore, Ms. Sanchez went on to state that her other concerns included: the
height of the domes, which exceed 27 feet; that the glass domes would reflect light;
potential soil contamination and the need for core sample tests; and the proposed
height of the wall. Lastly, Ms. Sanchez recommended that Council deny the proposed
zone variances, amendments, and and entitlements requested by the applicant.

George Kivett, Lomita resident, stated that there were a lot of variances approved by
the Planning Commission, and to be approved by Council, and he asked that Council
approve the proposed project and close this sad chapter in Lomita’s history.

Bilal Vashi, Lomita resident, stated that a lot of compromises had been made by the
Islamic Center of the South Bay, and it seems as if it is still not enough, as even more
conditions are being put in place. Mr. Voshi asked Council to make the right decision.

Dr. Reinhard Krauss, member of the public, stated that he teaches Christianity,
Judaism, and Islam at UCLA, and asked Council to approve the project in order to

  Page 8
 provide the Islamic Center of the South Bay with the opportunity to exercise their
religion in an adequate facility.

Henry Sanchez, City Councilmember, but speaking as private citizen of Lomita, stated
that his primary concern deals with the fact that the proposed building does not fit the
zoning and architectural style of the neighborhood. Mr. Sanchez went on to express his
other concerns regarding the proposed project, which included: that the proposed
domes would reflect light; the large size of the building; the fact that the lights will be
constantly on during Ramadan; and the associated noise. Furthermore, Mr. Sanchez
recommended that the doors be closed during Ramadan in order to reduce noise, and
that no sound should come from the minaret.

Lawson Pedigo, Lomita resident, stated that this should not be a religious issue, and
recommended that Council approve the project and make any necessary compromises.

Linda Rapoza, Lomita resident, recommended that the proposed project be built on a
smaller scale, which would be more appealing to the area.

Mayor Estrada closed the Public Hearing.

In response to Councilmember Traina’s questions as to why the current zoning allows
the building to be built to a height of 35 feet, and why the applicant is asking for a
variance for 32 feet, City Attorney Hogin responded that under current commercial/retail
zoning height is permitted up to 35 feet, however, the current building is a non-
conforming religious facility in commercial/retail zoning, therefore, rezoning to
residential would make the property conforming under the City’s Zoning Code, but the
permitted residential zoning height is 27 feet, so the variance is needed for the domes
and minaret, which go up to 32 and 33 feet in height respectively.

In response to Councilmember Traina’s question regarding the depth of the core
samples taken, Mr. Patel responded that core samples were taken down to 30 feet.

Councilmember Traina stated that City Council’s job is to keep emotion out of the
situation, to not make this a religious issue, and to make a good decision that would
satisfy both sides. Councilmember Traina went on to say that the height of the wall still
seems to be an issue, and also recommended that the applicant look into non-reflective
glass material for the roof and domes in order to reduce glare.

Councilmember Gazeley stated that he previously voted to deny the project as Planning
Commissioner, however, with all the proposed changes and improvements, the project
looks good. Councilmember Gazeley also commented on the currently inadequate
conditions of the Islamic Center of the South Bay. Lastly, Councilmember Gazeley

  Page 9
 recommended that the height of the wall and glass material be taken into considered in
order to satisfy the concerns of residents.

Councilmember Savidan agreed with both Councilmembers Traina and Gazeley, and
thanked everyone for coming out and giving their testimony, which he stated was
compelling on both sides. Furthermore, Councilmember Savidan stated that the Islamic
Center of the South Bay has a reasonable request to build a suitable facility in which to
exercise their religion, and that the Islamic Center has been a good neighbor for almost
30 years.

Councilmember Savidan moved to approve the recommendations from staff as
presented, adopt the associated resolutions, and introduce the ordinances with the
following three changes to the Conditional Use Permit and Variance resolutions: that
non-reflective glass be installed on the surface of the roof; that the height of the walls be
a minimum of seven feet, but a maximum of 12 feet, and be at least at the same level,
or taller than, the doors; and that only two domes be 32 feet in height. Councilmember
Traina seconded the motion, which carried unanimously.

ADJOURNMENT

Meeting adjourned in memory of Donna Hayes at 10:03 p.m.

Respectfully Submitted,

__________________________________
Lena Shumway, Assistant City Clerk, CMC
